reviews.scope: Naming triangle sides, angles, vertices and their correspondence
reviews.reason: Applying the law means matching each side with its opposite angle and finding the angle between two sides. That uses the basic-element vocabulary of triangles. Classifying triangles by sides or angles is not needed.

reviews.scope: Stating the identity and computing a third side from known cosines
reviews.reason: General application starts from the stated identity. Computing with cosine 0 or 1/2 is a special case of computing with any allowed cosine. So mastering the general node already includes everything in the basic node.

The unit-circle definition explains why obtuse angles have negative cosines and how a supplementary turn relates to the included angle. However, many tasks give the cosine or recover it algebraically from side data.
reviews.counterexample: A learner can be taught cos(180-x) = -cos x directly and then treat cosines as given numbers within (-1,1).

reviews.scope: Numerical substitutions involving radicals and approximations
reviews.reason: Numerical problems often produce square roots when recovering side lengths, so radical arithmetic helps. Integer-data and symbolic elimination tasks, and unsimplified sqrt answers, avoid the mixed-radical and approximation criteria.
reviews.counterexample: Sides 3, 5, 7 give cos C = -1/2 using only rational arithmetic.

reviews.scope: Meaning of a sphere's center and radius
reviews.reason: Every contact condition, whether radius sum, radius difference or distance to a plane, is stated through sphere centers and radii. Without these elements the tangency equations have no meaning. Cylinder and cone content is irrelevant.

The coordinate distance formula is one way to evaluate distances between centers. Synthetic right-triangle arguments that combine horizontal separation and vertical rise reach the same relations without coordinates.
reviews.counterexample: Stacked spheres on a plane can be solved with a plane Pythagorean triangle formed by the centers.

reviews.reason: Congruence classes give a compact proof that a repeating reply strategy works. Evaluating a finite game by backward induction tables needs no modular arithmetic, and a periodicity proof can use plain remainder reasoning.
reviews.counterexample: A pile of at most 20 with removals of 1 to 4 can be classified completely by a backward table.
